title: How Freak Shows Worked
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history of freak shows, from early human curiosities like Lazarus Colorado and his parasitic twin Johannes, through P. T. Barnum's exhibits (Joyce Heth, the Fiji Mermaid, General Tom Thumb) and rival Tom Norman, who toured with Joseph Merrick, the Elephant Man. They cover microcephalic performers Zip the Pinhead and Schlitzie, the 1932 film Freaks and its cast (Johnny Eck, Daisy and Violet Hilton, Harry and Daisy Earles), the decline of sideshows amid medical scrutiny, television, and the 1960s North Carolina complaint by Carol Grant, and close with listener mail about artificial photosynthesis following a Bill Gates episode.

segments.title: Opening banter and disclaimer
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode, note that outdated terms like freaks appear in historical quotes, and credit their sources.

segments.title: Origins of human curiosities
segments.summary: Definition of freak shows and early examples, including Lazarus Colorado and his parasitic twin Johannes, performing before King Charles I in the 1640s.

segments.title: P. T. Barnum's early career and Joyce Heth
segments.summary: Barnum's teenage lottery, his purchase of Joyce Heth, the false claim she was George Washington's nurse, and the anonymous hoax letter that boosted ticket sales.

segments.title: Fiji Mermaid and Levi Lyman
segments.summary: Barnum promoted the Fiji Mermaid, a fake creature leased from Japanese fishermen, with partner Levi Lyman posing as an English doctor; the pair later opened a Broadway museum.

segments.title: Tom Norman and Joseph Merrick
segments.summary: Tom Norman, Barnum's English counterpart known as the Silver King, toured with Joseph Merrick the Elephant Man; Frederick Treves criticized the exploitation and Norman defended his treatment of performers.

segments.title: Critics and the morality of audiences
segments.summary: Historian Henry Mayhew condemned freak shows in 1860 and placed blame on the gawking audiences rather than performers.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break with a brief Van Halen reference.

segments.title: Sideshow formats, recruitment, and pickled punks
segments.summary: Description of the ten-in-one show, advertising adults-only performances, pickled punk displays, and how managers recruited children and purchased performers from poor families.

segments.title: Tom Thumb and Charles Stratton
segments.summary: Barnum recruited his distant cousin Charles Stratton, billed as General Tom Thumb, who became an international celebrity, performed for Queen Victoria, and earned substantial wealth; Barnum's later financial troubles are noted.

segments.title: Zip the Pinhead and Schlitzie
segments.summary: Zip (William Henry Johnson) was billed as a missing link and likely was not microcephalic; Schlitzie, a performer beloved by colleagues, was billed as a woman and appeared in Freaks.

segments.title: The 1932 film Freaks and its cast
segments.summary: Todd Browning's pre-Code film Freaks, featuring Johnny Eck, Daisy and Violet Hilton, and Harry and Daisy Earles; Schlitzie's later life and the decline of sideshows with medical scrutiny, television, and the 1960s North Carolina complaint.
